p.seg: *Jì Piān* (The Laying Plans)
Sūnzǐ said:
War is
a matter of great importance to the state;
the ground of life and death,
the path to survival or ruin.
It is mandatory to examine it.
Therefore, assess it through five factors,
compare it through calculations,
and thereby seek out its realities:
The first is *dào* (道, the Way),
Second is tiān (天, heaven),
third is dì (地, earth),
fourth is jiàng (將, the general),
fifth is fǎ (法, law).
Dào (道, the Way) is
making the people's will in agreement with the ruler's,
therefore, one can face death with them,
one can share life with them,
and they will not fear danger.
Tiān (天, heaven) is
yīn yáng (陰陽), cold and heat, seasonal timing.
Dì (地, earth) is
height and depth, distance, hazardous and easy terrain, wide and narrow spaces, life and death.
Jiàng (將, the general) is
zhì (智, wisdom), xìn (信, trustworthiness), rén (仁, benevolence), yǒng (勇, courage), yán (嚴, strictness).
Fǎ (法, law) is
regulations and systems, official paths, the ruler's use.
Of all these five,
no general should be ignorant.
Knowing them leads to victory,
not knowing them leads to defeat.
Therefore, compare them by planning
and seek out their true conditions,
saying:
Which ruler possesses the Dào (道, the Way)?
Which general is more capable?
Which side gains the advantages of tiān dì (天地, heaven and earth)?
Which side's laws and orders are better implemented?
Which side's army is stronger?
Which side's soldiers are better trained?
Which side's rewards and punishments are clearer?
By these, I can know victory or defeat.
If the general listens to my plans,
and implements them, he will surely win;
retain him.
If the general does not listen to my plans,
and implements them, he will surely lose;
dismiss him.
Once the advantages of the plan are heard,
then create a *shì* (strategic advantage) for him,
to assist him externally.
*Shì* is
adapting your authority according to the advantageous situation.
Warfare is
a method of deception.
Therefore, when capable, feign incapacity;
when employing forces, feign not using them;
when near, feign being far away;
when far away, feign being near;
entice them with profit;
take them when they are in disarray;
prepare against them when they are strong;
avoid them when they are powerful;
Infuriate them and harass them;
act humbly and make them arrogant;
let them be at ease and tire them out;
appear intimate and keep them at a distance;
attack where they are unprepared;
strike when they do not expect it.
These are the keys to victory for a military strategist,
and cannot be transmitted beforehand.
Now,
if, before a battle, calculations in the temple show victory,
it is because many factors contributing to victory have been accounted for.
If, before a battle, calculations in the temple show no victory,
it is because few factors contributing to victory have been accounted for.
With many factors accounted for, one wins;
with few factors accounted for, one does not win;
how much less so with no calculations at all!
I observe things from this perspective,
and the outcome of victory or defeat becomes clear.
*Zuòzhàn Piān* (Waging War)
Sūnzǐ said:
In general, the method of using troops is as follows:
a thousand four-horse chariots,
a thousand supply wagons,
one hundred thousand armored soldiers,
transporting provisions a thousand *lǐ*;
then the expenses within and without the country, the costs of entertaining envoys,
Materials like glue and lacquer,
and the provision of chariots and armor,
cost a thousand gold pieces daily;
only then can an army of one hundred thousand be raised.
When employing them in war,
victory is desired, but if prolonged,
then weapons will become dull and morale will be sapped.
If attacking cities,
then strength will be exhausted.
If keeping an army in the field for a long time,
then the resources of the state will be insufficient.
Now, if weapons become dull and morale is sapped,
strength is exhausted and wealth is depleted,
then the feudal lords will take advantage of the weakness and rise up.
Even if there are wise men,
they will not be able to rectify the situation afterward.
Therefore, in war, one has heard of clumsy speed,
but never seen cleverness that lasts long.
That a nation benefits from prolonged war
has never happened.
Therefore, if one does not fully understand the harm of using troops,
then one cannot fully understand the benefit of using troops.
Those skilled in using troops
do not conscript a second time,
nor transport grain more than three times.
They obtain supplies from their own country
but rely on the enemy for food,
Therefore, the army's food supply can be sufficient.
When a state becomes impoverished due to the army, it is because of
long-distance transport.
Long-distance transport impoverishes the people.
Being near the army allows for selling at high prices.
Selling at high prices depletes the people's wealth.
When wealth is depleted, they are urgently pressed into corvée labor.
Strength exhausted, wealth depleted, the Central Plains
become internally emptied at home.
The people's expenses
are reduced by seven-tenths.
The state's expenses,
broken carts, exhausted horses,
armor, helmets, arrows, crossbows,
spears, shields, mantlets, and large shields,
hill oxen, and large carts,
are reduced by six-tenths.
Therefore, a wise general strives to take food from the enemy.
Taking one *zhōng* 鍾 of the enemy's food
is equivalent to twenty of our *zhōng*.
One *shí* 石 of the enemy's straw
is equivalent to twenty of our *shí*.
Therefore, to kill the enemy,
incite anger.
To seize the enemy's advantages,
These are the spoils of war.
Therefore, in chariot warfare,
if you capture ten or more chariots,
reward the one who captured them first,
and change their flags and banners.
Mix the captured chariots with your own and use them;
treat the captured soldiers well and maintain them.
This is called "winning over the enemy and becoming stronger."
Thus, in war, speed is valued;
protracted campaigns are not.
Therefore, the general who understands warfare
is the arbiter of the people's fate,
and the master of the nation's security.
*Móu Gōng Piān* (Attack by Stratagem)
Sūnzǐ yuē:
In general, the best policy in war
is to capture the enemy state intact;
to destroy it is inferior.
To capture the enemy army intact is best;
to destroy it is inferior.
To capture a brigade intact is best;
to destroy it is inferior.
To capture a battalion intact is best;
to destroy it is inferior.
To capture a squad intact is best;
Next in order is to break up alliances.
Therefore, to fight in a hundred battles and win a hundred victories
is not the most excellent of excellent things;
to subdue the enemy's army without fighting
is the most excellent of excellent things.
Thus, the best policy in war is to attack the enemy's plans;
next is to attack his alliances;
next is to attack his army;
and the worst is to attack fortified cities.
The method of attacking cities
is only employed when there is no alternative.
To prepare shielded wagons (lǔ)
and battering rams (fényùn), and to gather all sorts of equipment,
requires three months to complete.
To build up earthworks (jù yīn)
requires another three months.
If the general, unable to control his impatience, orders his troops to swarm up the walls like ants,
killing one-third of his soldiers,
while the city still remains untaken,
this is the calamity of attacking.
Therefore, a skilled commander
subdues the enemy's army without fighting, captures his cities without attacking,
and destroys his state without protracted operations.
He must contend for the whole empire with his forces intact.
Thus, his army is not worn out, and his gains are complete.
This is the art of attacking by stratagem (móugōng).
Therefore, the principles of employing troops are:
If ten times the enemy's strength, surround them;
if five times, attack them;
if double, divide them;
if equal, be able to fight them;
if fewer, be able to flee from them;
if weaker, be able to avoid them.
Therefore, a small force that stubbornly resists
will be captured by a large enemy.
Now, the general (jiàng) is
the support of the state;
if the support is comprehensive, the state will surely be strong;
if the support is flawed, the state will surely be weak.
Thus, there are three ways in which a ruler brings trouble upon the army:
not knowing that the army should not advance and yet ordering it to advance,
not knowing that the army should not retreat and yet ordering it to retreat—
this is called hobbling the army.
Not understanding the affairs of the three armies
and yet interfering in their administration,
then the soldiers will be confused;
not understanding the authority of the three armies
and yet interfering in their command,
then the soldiers will be doubtful.
If the three armies are both confused and doubtful,
then the troubles from the feudal lords will arrive.
This is called throwing the army into disorder and inviting victory.
Therefore, there are five ways to know victory:
Knowing when to fight and when not to fight leads to victory;
Understanding how to use both large and small forces leads to victory;
Having the same desires and intentions between superiors and inferiors leads to victory;
Being prepared to face the unprepared leads to victory;
Having a general who is capable and not interfered with by the ruler leads to victory.
These five are
the way to know victory.
Therefore it is said:
If you know both yourself and your enemy, you will not be in danger in a hundred battles;
if you only know yourself but not your enemy, you will win one and lose one;
if you know neither yourself nor your enemy, you will be in danger in every battle.
*Xíng Piān* ("Shape")
Sūnzǐ said:
Those skilled in war in ancient times
first made themselves invincible,
and then waited for the enemy to become vulnerable.
Invincibility lies with oneself,
vulnerability lies with the enemy.
Therefore, those skilled in war
can make themselves invincible,
but cannot make the enemy vulnerable.
Therefore it is said:
Victory can be known, but it cannot be forced.
To be invincible
is to defend;
to be able to win
is to attack.
Defense implies inadequacy;
attack implies abundance.
One skilled in defense
hides beneath the lowest depths;
one skilled in attack
moves above the highest heavens.
Thus, one can preserve oneself and achieve complete victory.
To perceive victory when it is no more than what everyone else knows is not the best of good strategies;
to win a battle and have the world say "well done" is not the best of good strategies.
Thus, lifting an autumn feather is not considered strength;
seeing the sun and moon is not considered sharp vision;
hearing thunder is not considered acute hearing.
The ancients' so-called skilled warriors
win where it is easy to win.
Therefore, the victory of a skilled warrior
brings no reputation for wisdom,
and no credit for courage.
Therefore, his victory is not a fluke.
One who does not err
positions himself where victory is certain,
To conquer is to defeat what is already defeated.
Therefore, a skilled warrior
establishes himself in a position where defeat is impossible,
and does not miss the opportunity to defeat the enemy.
Thus, a victorious army first ensures victory and then seeks battle,
while a defeated army first engages in battle and then hopes for victory.
Those skilled in employing troops cultivate the Way and preserve the laws,
therefore they are able to control the administration of victory and defeat.
Military methods:
first is measurement (dù),
second is estimation (liàng),
third is calculation (shù),
fourth is balancing (chēng),
fifth is victory (shèng).
The ground gives rise to measurement,
measurement gives rise to estimation,
estimation gives rise to calculation,
calculation gives rise to balancing,
balancing gives rise to victory.
Therefore, a victorious army is like weighing zhū with yì,
while a defeated army is like weighing yì with zhū.
The victory of the victorious
over the people is like releasing pent-up water into a ravine a thousand *rèn* deep;
it is [a matter of] disposition (xíng).
"Shì Piān"
Sūnzǐ said:
To govern a large multitude is like governing a small one;
it is a matter of divisions and numbers.
To fight a large multitude is like fighting a small one;
it is a matter of forms and names.
That the mass of the three armies
can be made to certainly receive the enemy without defeat
is due to the odd and the even.
That the force of arms, when applied,
is like hurling a rock against eggs
is a matter of utilizing emptiness and fullness.
In all battles,
one engages with the orthodox,
and wins with the unorthodox.
Therefore, one skilled at sending forth the unorthodox
is as inexhaustible as Heaven and Earth,
as unending as the rivers and streams.
Ending and beginning again
is like the sun and moon;
dying and being reborn
is like the four seasons.
There are no more than five musical notes;
yet the variations of these five notes
cannot be entirely heard.
There are no more than five colors;
yet the variations of these five colors
One cannot see them all;
Flavors are no more than five,
Yet the variations of these five flavors
Cannot be fully tasted;
Military formations are no more than qí (奇) and zhèng (正) (unorthodox and orthodox),
Yet the variations of qí (奇) and zhèng (正)
Cannot be completely exhausted.
Qí (奇) and zhèng (正) produce each other,
Like a circle without end,
Who can exhaust them?
The swiftness of rushing water,
To the point that it carries away stones,
Is due to momentum (shì 勢);
The swiftness of a bird of prey,
To the point that it shatters its prey,
Is due to timing (jié 節).
Therefore, one who is skilled in warfare
Has dangerous momentum (shì 勢),
And concise timing (jié 節);
His momentum (shì 勢) is like drawing a crossbow,
His timing (jié 節) is like releasing the trigger.
Though appearing confused and disordered,
Fighting is not truly chaotic;
Though appearing turbid and undifferentiated,
The formation is circular and cannot be defeated.
Disorder arises from order,
Cowardice arises from courage,
Weakness arises from strength.
Order and disorder are a matter of numerical calculation (shù yě);
courage and cowardice are a matter of disposition (shì yě);
Are a matter of momentum (shì 勢);
strength and weakness are a matter of physical form (xíng yě).
Are a matter of disposition (xíng 形).
Therefore, one skilled at moving the enemy
presents a shape (xíng zhī) to them,
and the enemy will certainly follow it;
offers them something (yǔ zhī),
and the enemy will certainly take it.
Move them with profit,
and lie in wait for them with troops.
Therefore, one skilled in battle
seeks it in disposition (shì),
and does not demand it of men.
Therefore, he is able to select men and rely on disposition (shì).
One who relies on disposition (shì),
when he battles with men,
is like rolling logs and stones.
The nature of logs and stones:
when at rest, they are still;
when in danger, they move;
when square, they stop;
when round, they roll.
Therefore, the disposition (shì) of one skilled in battle
is like rolling round stones from a thousand-仞 (rèn) mountain:
This concerns *shì* (勢, strategic advantage).
*Xū Shí Piān* (虛實篇, Weaknesses and Strengths).
Sūnzǐ (孫子) said:
In general, those who first occupy the battlefield and await the enemy are at ease;
those who arrive at the battlefield later and hasten into battle are fatigued.
Therefore, those skilled in war
bring others to them and are not brought to others.
To be able to make the enemy come of their own accord,
benefit them;
to be able to prevent the enemy from coming,
Therefore, if the enemy is at ease, be able to weary them;
if they are full, be able to make them hungry;
if they are settled, be able to make them move.
Go where they will not rush,
rush where they do not expect.
To march a thousand *lǐ* (里) without fatigue,
is to march through uninhabited territory;
to attack and surely take,
to defend and surely hold,
Therefore, those skilled at attacking,
the enemy does not know where to defend;
those skilled at defending,
The enemy does not know where I will attack.
Subtle, so subtle,
to the point of being without form;
mysterious, so mysterious,
harm them.
is to attack where they do not defend;
is to defend where they do not attack.
to the point of being without sound;
therefore, I am able to control the enemy's fate.
Advancing and being unstoppable is
striking at their emptiness;
retreating and being unpursuable is
being swift and unattainable.
Therefore, if I desire to fight,
even if the enemy has high ramparts and deep moats,
they will have no choice but to fight with me;
it is because I am attacking what they must rescue.
If I do not desire to fight,
drawing a line on the ground and defending it,
the enemy will not be able to fight with me;
it is because I am leading them away from where they intend to go.
Therefore, if I cause the enemy to take shape while I remain without form,
then I am concentrated while the enemy is divided.
I am concentrated as one, while the enemy is divided into ten;
therefore, I can attack them with ten against one.
Then I am numerous while the enemy is few;
being able to strike the few with the many
means that the place where I engage in battle will be limited.
The place where I will engage in battle cannot be known;
If the enemy's intentions are unknowable, then their preparations will be extensive;
if the enemy's preparations are extensive,
then those with whom we engage in battle will be few.
Therefore, if one prepares at the front, the rear will be weak;
if one prepares at the rear, the front will be weak;
if one prepares on the left, the right will be weak;
if one prepares on the right, the left will be weak;
if one prepares everywhere, then everywhere will be weak.
To be few
is the result of preparing against others;
to be many
is the result of making others prepare against oneself.
Therefore, knowing the place of battle
and knowing the day of battle,
one can converge from a thousand *lǐ* to fight;
not knowing the place of battle
and not knowing the day of battle,
then the left cannot save the right,
the right cannot save the left,
the front cannot save the rear,
the rear cannot save the front,
how much less so when those distant are tens of *lǐ* away,
and those near are several *lǐ* away!
Judging by my calculations,
even if the soldiers of the Yuè rén (越人) are numerous,
what advantage would it give them in victory or defeat?
Therefore, it is said:
Victory can be created;
even if the enemy is numerous,
they can be made not to fight.
Thus, assess them and know the plans of gains and losses;
provoke them and know the principles of movement and stillness;
shape them and know the ground of life and death;
test them and know where there is surplus and deficiency.
Therefore, the ultimate form of deploying troops
is to reach formlessness;
in formlessness,
even deep spies cannot see,
and the wise cannot scheme.
Based on the (enemy's) form, deploy victory among the multitude,
the multitude cannot know (how you do it);
everyone knows the form by which I achieve victory,
but no one knows the form by which I create victory.
Therefore, his victories in battle are not repeated,
but he responds to forms infinitely.
Now, the military disposition is like water.
The form of water
avoids heights and rushes downwards;
the form of the military
avoids strength and strikes weakness.
Water's flow is determined by the terrain;
an army's victory is determined by the enemy.
Therefore, armies have no constant formation,
and water has no constant shape.
The one who can achieve victory by changing in accordance with the enemy
is called divine.
Therefore, the Five Elements have no constant victor, the Four Seasons have no constant position,
the days have short and long periods,
and the moon has waxing and waning phases.
"Military Contest"
ST Sūnzǐ yuē:
In general, the method of employing troops is such that,
after the general receives his orders from the ruler,
assembles the army and gathers the masses,
and camps in concert,
nothing is more difficult than contending for advantage.
The difficulty in contending for advantage
lies in making the indirect direct,
and turning calamity into advantage.
Therefore, make a roundabout route and entice the enemy with profit,
setting out after others,
but arriving before them—
this is someone who understands the plan of indirectness and directness.
Thus, contending for advantage can bring benefit,
but contending for advantage can also bring danger.
To move the entire army to vie for advantage will result in failure to reach the objective.
To leave the army behind and vie for advantage will result in the loss of baggage and supplies.
Therefore, to roll up the armor and rush forward,
not stopping day or night,
advancing at double speed,
and contending for advantage at a distance of one hundred *lǐ*,
one may capture three generals.
The strong will arrive first,
the weary will lag behind,
and according to this method, only one-tenth of the force will arrive.
To contend for advantage at a distance of fifty *lǐ*,
one might lose the commander of the upper army,
and according to this method, only half the force will arrive.
To contend for advantage at a distance of thirty *lǐ*,
two-thirds of the force will arrive.
Therefore, an army without baggage and supplies is doomed;
an army without provisions is doomed;
an army without stores is doomed.
Therefore, one who does not know the plans of the feudal lords cannot make alliances in advance;
one who does not know the terrain of mountains, forests, dangerous obstacles, and marshes
cannot conduct military operations;
and one who does not use local guides
cannot gain the advantages of terrain.
Thus, warfare is established on deception,
it is motivated by advantage,
and it changes through division and combination.
To vary tactics by dispersing and uniting is essential.
Therefore, his speed is like the wind,
his slowness like the forest;
plundering like fire,
immobility like a mountain,
inscrutability like the shadow,
movement like thunder.
In plundering a village, divide the troops;
in expanding territory, divide the profits;
act by weighing the circumstances.
He who first knows the plan of indirectness and directness wins;
this is the method of military competition.
The *Jūn Zhèng* says:
"When words cannot be heard,
use gongs and drums;
when faces cannot be seen,
use banners and flags."
Now, gongs, drums, banners, and flags
are the means of unifying the ears and eyes of the soldiers;
when the soldiers are focused and united,
then the brave cannot advance alone,
and the cowardly cannot retreat alone.
This is the method of employing the masses.
Therefore, in night battles, there are many fires and drums;
in daytime battles, there are many banners and flags.
This is how to change people's perceptions.
Thus, the spirit of the entire army can be seized,
and the mind of the general can be seized.
Therefore, the morning spirit is sharp,
the daytime spirit is sluggish,
and the evening spirit is homeward-bound.
Therefore, those skilled in using troops
avoid their sharp spirit
and strike when their sluggish spirit is returning.
This is governing spirit.
To await disorder with order,
to await clamor with stillness:
this is governing the mind.
To await those who are near for those who are far,
to await those who are rested for those who are weary,
to await those who are full for those who are hungry:
this is governing strength.
Do not intercept banners that are aligned,
do not strike formations that are imposing.
This is governing change.
Therefore, the methods of employing troops are:
do not attack high ground,
do not oppose those with their backs to hills,
do not follow those feigning defeat,
Do not attack a spirited force.
Do not eat bait troops.
Do not block a returning army.
When besieging a force, leave an outlet.
Do not press a desperate foe.
These are the principles of employing troops.
*The Nine Variations*
Sūnzǐ said:
In general, the method of employing troops is this:
the general receives his orders from the ruler,
assembles the army and gathers the masses.
On broken ground, do not encamp;
on intersecting ground, establish alliances;
on isolated ground, do not linger;
on surrounded ground, devise a plan;
on death ground, fight.
There are roads not to take;
there are armies not to strike;
there are cities not to assault;
there is ground not to contest;
there are commands of the ruler that are not to be obeyed.
Therefore, a general who understands the advantages of the nine variations knows how to employ troops.
A general who does not understand the advantages of the nine variations,
even if he knows the terrain,
cannot gain the advantage of the ground.
One cannot gain the advantages of terrain.
Managing the army without knowing the art of the Nine Variations,
Even if one knows the Five Advantages,
One cannot get the best use of one's men.
Therefore, the considerations of a wise commander
Must be mixed with both advantages and disadvantages.
By mixing with advantages, affairs can be made reliable;
By mixing with disadvantages, troubles can be resolved.
Therefore, bend the feudal lords with harm;
Employ the feudal lords with labor;
Drive the feudal lords with profit.
Therefore, the principle of employing troops
Is not to rely on the enemy not coming,
But to rely on having the means to meet him.
Not to rely on the enemy not attacking,
But to rely on having positions that are unassailable.
Therefore, a general has five dangerous faults:
Being reckless, he can be killed; being cowardly, he can be captured;
Being quick-tempered, he can be insulted;
Being concerned with his reputation, he can be disgraced;
Being overly fond of his people, he can be troubled.
All these five are
The faults of a general,
And the calamities of employing troops.
To defeat an army and kill its generals
is certainly due to five dangerous faults,
which must be carefully examined.
"Maneuvering the Army"
Sūnzǐ said:
In general, when stationing an army and confronting the enemy,
cross mountains and stay near valleys,
look for high ground that is well-situated,
do not climb hills to attack,
this is how to station an army in mountainous terrain.
When crossing water, be sure to stay far from the water;
if the enemy crosses water to come,
do not meet them in the water,
but let half of them cross and then attack, it is advantageous;
if you wish to fight,
do not face the enemy attached to the water;
look for high ground that is well-situated,
do not face the water's current,
this is how to station an army on water.
When crossing salt marshes,
be sure to leave quickly and do not linger.
If you engage the enemy in the middle of a salt marsh,
be sure to rely on water and grass
and have your back to many trees.
When banners and flags move about,
it signifies disorder;
when officers are angry,
Weariness.
Providing millet and meat to the horses and soldiers, the army having no
suspended cooking pots, and not
returning to their quarters—
these are desperate enemies.
Speaking earnestly and harmoniously,
and speaking slowly to others—
this means losing the support of the masses.
Frequent rewards—
this indicates straits.
Frequent punishments—
this indicates being besieged. Acting violently at first and then fearing
their own troops—this is the height of incompetence.
Those who come to apologize indicate a desire to rest.
Soldiers advancing angrily to meet the enemy,
but for a long time not engaging,
nor withdrawing from each other—
one must carefully observe them.
It is not necessarily better to have more troops;
the key is not to advance recklessly.
Rushing around and deploying chariots—
this indicates an agreed-upon engagement (qī).
Advancing halfway and then retreating halfway—
this is a lure.
Those who stand leaning on their staffs—
are hungry.
One who draws water and drinks first is thirsty.
One who sees profit but does not advance is weary.
Where birds gather is empty.
One who shouts at night is afraid.
If the army is in disarray, the general is not respected.
Birds taking flight indicate an ambush.
Startled beasts indicate an attack.
Dust that rises high and sharply indicates the approach of chariots.
Dust that is low and wide indicates the approach of infantry.
Dust that is scattered and spreads out in lines indicates wood gatherers.
Dust that is sparse and moves back and forth indicates the encampment of troops.
When words are humble and increasingly detailed, it indicates an advance.
When words are forceful and accompanied by a forward drive, it indicates a retreat.
Light chariots coming out first and positioning themselves on the flank indicate a battle formation (chén 陳).
To request peace without a prior agreement is a stratagem.
Generally, places with impassable ravines,
tiānjǐng (natural pit traps),
tiānláo (natural prisons),
tiānluó (natural nets),
tiānxiàn (natural pitfalls),
tiānxì (natural crevices),
must be left quickly,
do not approach them.
We keep distant from them,
the enemy approaches them;
we face them,
the enemy turns its back on them.
When an army marches and encounters dangerous obstacles, stagnant pools, reeds, rushes, mountains, forests, or dense thickets,
be sure to carefully search them thoroughly,
these are the places where hidden spies reside.
When the enemy is near but remains quiet,
they are relying on their dangerous position.
When they are far away but send challenges,

*Dì Xíng Piān* (Terrain)
Sūnzǐ (孫子) said:
Terrain can be categorized as accessible,
entangling,
branching,
narrow,
precipitous,
and distant.
Where I can go and
If they can come,
it is called "accessible";
in an "accessible" terrain,
first occupy the sunny high ground,
benefiting the grain supply route,
and fighting will be advantageous.
One can go,
but it is difficult to return,
it is called "entangling";
in an "entangling" terrain,
if the enemy is unprepared,
go out and defeat them;
if the enemy is prepared,
go out but do not prevail,
and it is difficult to return,
it is disadvantageous.
If we go out and it is disadvantageous,
and they go out and it is disadvantageous;
it is called "stalemate";
in a "stalemate" terrain,
even if the enemy is able to gain an advantage over us,
we must not go out.
Lead them away,
causing the enemy to come out halfway and strike them,
it is advantageous.
In a "narrow" terrain,
if we occupy it first,
be sure to fill it and wait for the enemy;
If the enemy occupies a position first,
if it is full (of advantages), do not follow him;
if it is not full (of advantages), follow him.
In the case of dangerous terrain,
occupy it first,
be sure to occupy the high, sunny ground to await the enemy;
if the enemy occupies it first,
lead your troops away and leave,
do not follow him.
In the case of distant terrain,
if the situation is balanced, it is difficult to challenge,
and fighting will be disadvantageous.
All these six are
the principles of terrain,
the utmost responsibility of the general,
which must be carefully observed.
Thus, soldiers may flee (zǒu),
become lax (chí),
become trapped (xiàn),
collapse (bēng),
become disordered (luàn),
or be defeated (běi).
All these six are
not natural disasters,
but the faults of the general.
When the situation is balanced, but you attack ten with one,
it is called fleeing (zǒu);
when the soldiers are strong but the officers are weak,
it is called laxness (chí);
when the officers are strong but the soldiers are weak,
it is called becoming trapped (xiàn);
when senior officers are angry and disobedient,
encountering the enemy, they resentfully fight on their own,
and the general does not know their capabilities,
it is called "collapse" (bēng);
when the general is weak and not strict,
the instructions and teachings are unclear,
the officers and soldiers are inconsistent,
and the formation of troops is disorganized,
it is called "chaos" (luàn);
when the general cannot anticipate the enemy,
meets a few against many,
attacks the strong with the weak,
and the troops have no select vanguard,
it is called "defeat" (běi).
All these six situations
are the paths to defeat.
They are the ultimate responsibility of the general,
and must be carefully observed.
Now, terrain
is the assistant to the military.
To assess the enemy and determine victory,
calculate the perilous, constricted, far, and near places
is the way of a superior general.
Knowing this and using it in battle guarantees victory;
not knowing this and using it in battle guarantees defeat.
Therefore, if the way to fight ensures victory,
and the ruler says not to fight,
it is permissible to fight;
if the way to fight does not ensure victory,
and the ruler says to fight,
it is permissible not to fight.
Therefore, advancing without seeking fame,
retreating without avoiding blame,
only protecting the people,
and aligning benefits with the ruler,
is a treasure of the state.
View the soldiers as infants,

view the soldiers as beloved children,

To know that the enemy is vulnerable to attack,
to know that one's own troops are capable of attacking,
but not to know that the terrain is unsuitable for battle,
is only half the victory.
Therefore, one who understands warfare
acts without confusion,
and maneuvers without exhaustion.
Therefore, it is said:
Knowing the enemy and knowing yourself,
your victory will not be endangered;
knowing the heavens and knowing the earth,

*Jiǔ Dì Piān* (Nine Situations)
Sūnzǐ said:
The principles of employing troops are:
there is dispersive ground (*sàndì*),
there is facile ground (*qīngdì*),
there is contentious ground (*zhēngdì*),
there is communicative ground (*jiāodì*),
there is intersecting ground (*qúdì*),
there is heavy ground (*zhòngdì*),
there is entrapping ground (*yídì*),
there is surrounded ground (*wéidì*),
there is death ground (*sǐdì*).
When feudal lords fight on their own territory,
it is "dispersive ground";
when one enters the territory of others but not deeply,
it is "facile ground";
if we gain, it benefits us,
and if they gain, it also benefits them,
it is "contentious ground";
where we can go,
and they can come,
it is "communicating ground";
territory that borders three feudal lords,
where whoever arrives first gains the support of the populace,
is "key ground";
entering deeply into the territory of others,
with many walled cities behind,
is "grave ground";
traversing mountains,
dangerous passes,
marshy ground,
all difficult-to-travel roads,
is "entangling ground";
where the entry is narrow,
and the return is circuitous,
where the few can strike our many,
is "enclosed ground";
if fighting swiftly ensures survival,
and not fighting swiftly leads to destruction,
it is "desperate ground."
Therefore, in dispersive ground, do not fight;
in facile ground, do not halt;
in contentious ground, do not attack;
in communicative ground, do not cut off communications;
in intersecting ground, form alliances;
in heavy ground, plunder;
in entrapping ground, move on;
in encircled ground, devise stratagems;
in death ground, fight.
The
so-called skillful commanders of antiquity
were able to make the enemy's front and rear unable to coordinate,
the many and the few unable to rely on each other,
the noble and the base unable to rescue each other,
superiors and inferiors unable to support each other,
soldiers dispersed and not gathering,
troops joined together but not aligned.
Move when it is advantageous,
stop when it is not advantageous.
May I ask,
if the enemy comes with a large and well-ordered force,
how should one deal with them?
I say:
First seize what they love,
and they will listen.
The nature of war is to value speed,
Attack when they are unprepared;
take advantage of the unexpected routes;
strike where they are undefended.
Generally, the way to be a guest (invading army) is this:
When penetrating deeply, concentrate your forces;
the host will be unable to overcome you;
plunder in the rich fields;
your entire army will have enough to eat;
carefully nurture them but do not exhaust them;
unite their qi (vital energy), accumulate their strength,
maneuver your troops with calculated plans,
and be unfathomable.
Throw them where there is nowhere to go,
and they will die rather than flee north;
where can death not be found?
The soldiers will exert all their strength.
When soldiers are deeply entrapped, they are not afraid;
when there is nowhere to go, they become steadfast;
when penetrating deeply, they become cohesive;
when there is no other choice, they fight.
Therefore, your soldiers are disciplined without training,
successful without seeking,
close without promises,
and trustworthy without orders.
Suppress omens and dispel doubts; until death, there is nowhere else to go.
My soldiers have no excess wealth,
not because they dislike riches;
When there is no life left to spare,
it is not considered a bad end.
On the day orders are issued,
soldiers who are sitting weep, their lapels soaked with tears,
and those lying down weep, their tears mingling together.
To send them where there is no way to return,
that is the courage of Zhu Zhì (諸郅) and Cao Guì (曹劌).
Therefore, one who is good at using soldiers
is like the "Shuài Rán" (率然);
the "Shuài Rán"
is a snake from Mount Cháng Shān (常山).
Strike its head, and the tail will come to the rescue;
strike its tail, and the head will come to the rescue;
strike its middle, and the head and tail will both come to the rescue.
May I ask,
can soldiers be made like the "Shuài Rán"?
It is said:
Yes.
The people of Wú (吳) and the people of Yuè (越) hate each other,
but when they are in the same boat crossing a river and encounter wind,
they help each other as if they were the left and right hands.
Therefore, depending on holding horses back or burying chariot wheels
is not something to rely upon;
aligning courage as one
is the way of governance;
obtaining both strength and flexibility
is the principle of terrain.
Therefore, one who is good at using soldiers
Linking hands is only done when it's unavoidable.
is unavoidable.
The affairs of a general:
be still and profound,
be upright and orderly,
be able to deceive the eyes and ears of the soldiers,
making them ignorant;
change their tasks,
alter their plans,
making people unknowing;
change their dwelling places,

When the commander sets a date with them,

The variations of the nine terrains,

The principles of human nature,

Generally, the way of being a guest (or a subordinate),
if deep, then focused;
if shallow, then scattered.
Departing from one's country and crossing borders to act as a teacher (or a master),
is *jué dì* (isolated ground);
reaching a place with roads leading in all directions,

entering deeply,
is *zhòng dì* (vital ground);
entering shallowly,

is *wéi dì* (enclosed ground);

is *sǐ dì* (death ground).
Therefore, on scattered ground, I will unify their will;
on facile ground, I will make them connected;
on contested ground, I will hasten their rear;
on intersecting ground, I will be careful of their defenses;
on thoroughfare ground, I will strengthen their alliances;
on vital ground, I will continue to provide their food;
on broken ground, I will advance their path;
on enclosed ground, I will block their gaps;
on death ground, I will show them that there is no hope of survival.
Thus, the sentiment of soldiers:
when surrounded, they defend;
If driven to it, then fight;
if they overstep, then comply.
Therefore, one who does not know the plans of the feudal lords
cannot form alliances beforehand;
one who does not know the shapes of mountains, forests,
perilous passages,

one who does not employ local guides

If of these four or five matters,

Now, the army of a hegemon or king—
when attacking a large state,

when its威 wēi (power/majesty) is applied to the enemy,

Therefore, not contending for alliances throughout the world,
not fostering power throughout the world,
trusting in one's own selfishness,
and applying 威 wēi (power/majesty) to the enemy,
therefore their cities can be captured,
and their states can be destroyed.
Bestowing rewards without law,
issuing commands without governance,
assaulting the masses of the three armies
If you cause a single man
to err with an affair,
do not inform him with words;
if you cause him to err with profit,
do not inform him of the harm.
Throw him into a place of destruction, and then he will survive;
sink him into a place of death, and then he will live.
For when the masses are mired in harm,
then they can determine victory and defeat.
Therefore, in the affairs of war,
the key lies in conforming to and closely examining the enemy's intentions,
concentrating forces against a single point of the enemy,
killing the general from a thousand *lǐ* away.
This is what is meant by skillfully accomplishing matters.
Therefore, on the day of initiating policy,
level the passes and break the tallies,
do not allow their envoys to pass through.
Be resolute within the halls of government,
to execute your plans.
When the enemy opens a gap,
you must quickly enter it;
prioritize what they cherish;
subtly arrange a time with them;
follow the ink line and comply with the enemy,
in order to determine the war's affairs.
Therefore, in the beginning, be like a virgin;
when the enemy opens their gate.
Afterwards, be like a fleeing rabbit,
the enemy will not have time to resist.
*The Fire Attack*
Sūnzǐ said:
In general, there are five types of fire attack:
one is to burn people,
two is to burn supplies,
three is to burn baggage trains,
four is to burn storehouses,
five is to burn troop formations.
To conduct a fire attack, there must be a reason;
the tools for creating smoke and fire must be prepared in advance.
There is a time to ignite a fire;
there is a day to start a fire.
The time is when the weather is dry;
the day is when the moon is in the constellations Jī (箕), Bì (壁), Yì (翼), or Zhěn (軫),
because these four constellations
are the days when the wind arises.
In general, when conducting a fire attack,
one must respond accordingly to the changes of the five fires:
if the fire starts within,
then respond to it from without as soon as possible;
When fire breaks out and the troops remain calm,
wait and do not attack.
Let the fire reach its maximum intensity.
If it is possible to follow up with an attack, then do so;
if it is not possible, then cease.
Fire can be set from outside,
without waiting for it to originate from within;
launch it according to the timing.
If the fire is upwind,
do not attack downwind.
Daytime winds last long;
nighttime winds cease.
In general, an army must know the five variations of fire attacks
and use these principles to defend themselves.
Therefore, those who use fire to assist their attacks are enlightened;
those who use water to assist their attacks are strong.
Water can be used to isolate,
but it cannot be used to seize.
To win battles and capture territory, yet fail to consolidate the gains, is ominous.
This is called "wasteful delay" (fèi liú).
Therefore it is said:
An enlightened ruler considers this,
a good general cultivates this.
Do not move unless there is an advantage;
do not act unless something can be gained;
do not fight unless there is danger.
A ruler should not raise an army out of anger,
A general must not initiate war out of pique;
move only if it is advantageous,
and stop if it is not advantageous.
Anger can revert to joy,
vexation can revert to pleasure,
but a destroyed state cannot be restored,
and the dead cannot be brought back to life.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler is cautious about it,
and the good general is wary of it;
this is the way to secure the state and preserve the army.
"Using Spies"
Sūnzǐ said:
Generally, mobilizing an army of one hundred thousand,
going on a campaign of a thousand *lǐ*,
the expenses of the people,
the emoluments of the public treasury,
daily expenditures of a thousand gold pieces,
disturbances both at home and abroad,
fatigue on the roads,
and those unable to attend to their affairs—
amount to seven hundred thousand families.
To contend with each other for several years,
just to vie for victory in a single day,
while being stingy with ranks and stipends of one hundred gold pieces,
and being ignorant of the enemy's situation,
is the height of inhumanity;
such a one is no general of the people,
They are not assistants to the ruler,
nor are they masters of victory.
Therefore, enlightened rulers and wise generals,
in order to move and conquer others,
and achieve success beyond the ordinary,
rely on prior knowledge.
This prior knowledge
cannot be obtained from ghosts and spirits,
cannot be inferred from analogy,
and cannot be verified by calculation;
it must be obtained from people
who know the enemy's situation.
Therefore, there are five kinds of spies: there are yīnjiàn 因間 (local spies),
nèijiàn 內間 (inside spies),
fǎnjiàn 反間 (double agents),
sǐjiàn 死間 (expendable spies),
and shēngjiàn 生間 (living spies).
When these five kinds of spies are all employed,
and no one knows their operations, this is called divine manipulation – shénjì 神紀 –
the treasure of the ruler.
Yīnjiàn 因間 (local spies)
are employed by making use of their local connections.
Nèijiàn 內間 (inside spies)
are employed by making use of their official positions.
Fǎnjiàn 反間 (double agents)
are employed by making use of the enemy's spies.
Sǐjiàn 死間 (expendable spies)
To create deceptive appearances externally,
causing my spies to learn of them,
and transmit them to the enemy's spies;
living spies are
those who report back.
Therefore, of all affairs in the three armies,
none is more intimate than espionage,
no reward is more generous than that for espionage,
and no matter is more confidential than espionage.
Without sagacity and wisdom, one cannot employ spies;
without benevolence and righteousness, one cannot command spies;
without subtlety, one cannot obtain the truth from spies.
Subtle, indeed, subtle!
There is no place where espionage is not useful.
If matters of espionage are revealed before they are acted upon,
both the spy and the one informed shall be put to death.
In general, whatever army one desires to attack,
whatever city one desires to besiege,
whatever person one desires to kill,
one must first know the names of their defending general, their aides,
their messengers,
their gatekeepers,
and their personal attendants;
one must order my spies to seek and know them.
One must seek out the enemy's spies who come to spy on me,
Therefore, entice them with benefits,
lead them and let them lodge there;
thus, the counter-spy can be obtained and used.
Based on this, know him,
thus, the local spy
and the inside spy can be obtained and employed.
Based on this, know him,
thus, the doomed spy fabricates false information,
and can be sent to inform the enemy.
Based on this, know him,
thus, the living spy can be sent to report as scheduled.
The affairs of the five kinds of spies,
the ruler must know them.
Knowing them must depend on the counter-spy,
therefore the counter-spy must not be treated shabbily.
In the past, when the Yīn dynasty rose,
Yī Zhì 伊挚 was in the Xià 夏 dynasty;
when the Zhōu 周 dynasty rose,
Lǚ Yá 吕牙 was in the Yīn 殷 dynasty.
Therefore, only an enlightened ruler and a wise general can employ spies with supreme intelligence,
and will certainly achieve great merit.
This is the key to military affairs,
and is what the three armies rely on to move.
